title: Cannabis and Parenting: Safety, Storage and Honest Talks
h1: Parenting and Cannabis: A Practical Guide for Adults Who Use
metaDescription: Judgment-free help for parents who use cannabis: talking with kids by age, locked child-resistant storage, edible safety, and the times not to use at all.
excerpt: A practical, judgment-free guide for Michigan parents who use cannabis: what to tell your kids, how to store it, why edibles need extra care, and the lines that never move.
keyTakeaways: Leave cannabis in the package it came in, inside a locked box or cabinet, out of sight and reach.
Edibles are the biggest risk at home. If a child eats one, call Poison Help at 1-800-222-1222, or 911 if symptoms are serious.
Never drive impaired, and use only when another sober adult is in charge of the kids.
The CDC advises against cannabis during pregnancy and breastfeeding; talk with your doctor.
Give kids honest answers sized to their age, with one constant message: cannabis is for adults 21 and older.
body:
Cannabis and parenting questions usually come down to a few habits that never slip. Everything stays locked up, edibles stay out of reach, and a sober adult is always in charge. Your kids, meanwhile, get honest answers sized to their age. Michigan law has allowed adults 21 and older to use cannabis since 2018, and plenty of parents do. Here’s how to handle the questions they ask most, without judgment and without cutting corners.

## Why cannabis and parenting questions keep coming up

For many Michigan parents, cannabis now sits where a bottle of wine does: legal, adults-only and kept away from kids. The questions are practical. Should I tell my kids? Where do I keep it? What if my child gets into it? Can it affect custody?

The stakes are real. A study of U.S. poison center data found that reported edible exposures in children under 6 climbed from 207 in 2017 to 3,054 in 2021. Nearly all of them (97.7%) happened at home, and 22.7% of the children were admitted to a hospital.

## How to talk to kids about weed, age by age

You don’t owe your kids a confession, and it’s wise not to lie if they ask. Many families land in between: honest answers sized to the child’s age, given calmly, with one message that never changes. Cannabis is for adults.

### Young children

Keep it short and concrete: “That’s a grown-up thing, like beer or wine. It’s not for kids, and it can make kids very sick. If you ever find something like it, don’t touch it. Come get me.” Young children need a simple instruction and a reason, not a lecture.

### School-age kids

Kids in elementary and middle school hear about cannabis from friends, shows and signs, and they may ask you directly. Answer the question they asked. Explain that it’s legal for adults 21 and older, not for kids, and that adults who use it do so in private and in moderation. Ask what they’ve heard; it tells you what to correct.

### Teens

Teens can handle fuller facts, and they notice when a story doesn’t add up. Tell them what you do, why it’s an adults-only choice, and what the science says about their age group. The National Institute on Drug Abuse calls adolescence an important period of brain development. It also notes that starting younger raises the odds of a cannabis use disorder later in life. Make your expectations clear, including never riding with a driver who has used.

## Safe cannabis storage with kids at home

Storage is where cannabis and parenting meet every day. Build it in layers:

1. **Keep the package it came in.** Michigan rules require edibles to come in opaque, child-resistant packaging, resealable when there’s more than one serving. Labels carry a “Keep out of reach of children” warning and the Poison Control number. Repackaging throws all of that away.
2. **Lock it.** The CDC recommends a locked, childproof container kept out of children’s sight and reach. Michigan law also requires anything over 2.5 ounces at home to be kept behind a lock.
3. **Keep it out of sight.** High shelves get climbed. Store products away from food, medicine and anything a child might mistake them for.
4. **Lock up the extras.** Vape cartridges, leftover pre-rolls, ash and empty packaging count, too. Guests’ bags and coat pockets are a classic gap.

Our [storage guide](/blog/how-to-store-marijuana/) covers keeping products fresh once they’re secure.

## Edibles and child safety

Edibles are the biggest risk at home because they look like food. Michigan bans edibles shaped like people, animals or fruit and bars the word “candy” on packaging, but a gummy still looks like a gummy to a five-year-old. Keep edibles in their own locked box, never in the pantry, fridge or a dish on the counter, and don’t eat them in front of young children.

If a child eats an edible or any cannabis product:

1. Stay calm and take away anything left.
2. Call Poison Help at 1-800-222-1222 right away for guidance.
3. Call 911 instead if the child is hard to wake or having trouble breathing.
4. Keep the package. It tells medical staff what was eaten and how much THC it held.

Children who consume THC can become very sick, the CDC warns, with trouble walking, sitting up or breathing. In the poison-center study above, 70% of cases followed to a known outcome involved central nervous system depression, such as heavy drowsiness.

## Safety lines that don’t move

- **No driving impaired.** Michigan law doesn’t let anyone drive while impaired or use cannabis behind the wheel. That covers school runs and practice pickups.
- **A sober caregiver on duty.** If you’re the only adult responsible for the kids, skip it. Save cannabis for times when another sober adult is in charge.
- **No smoke or vapor around kids.** NIDA notes that secondhand cannabis smoke carries many of the same toxins as secondhand tobacco smoke, and children exposed at home have tested positive for cannabis. If you smoke, do it outdoors on your own property, away from the kids and open windows.
- **Pregnancy and breastfeeding.** The CDC recommends against cannabis during pregnancy and encourages breastfeeding parents to avoid it entirely, since chemicals from cannabis can pass into breast milk. If you’re pregnant, planning a pregnancy or nursing, talk with your doctor.

## For medical patients who are parents

Some parents hold a Michigan medical marijuana card, which requires a physician’s certification. The message to kids, especially teens, stays the same with one addition. Your use follows a decision made with a doctor, for an adult, and it doesn’t make cannabis safe for a developing brain. Avoid mixed signals by keeping your products locked like everything else that’s adults-only. If you’re considering registering, we explain [how Michigan’s medical card works](/getting-a-medical-card/).

## Cannabis stigma, parents and the wine-glass double standard

A parent with a glass of wine at dinner rarely gets a second look, while a parent who uses cannabis can feel judged for a similar adult choice. You don’t need to win that argument. Hold yourself to the same standards either way: no impaired caregiving, locked storage, moderation and honest answers.

If relatives or other parents raise it, a calm “It’s legal, it’s locked up, and I don’t use when I’m in charge of the kids” usually settles it. And in Michigan, legal use alone isn’t grounds to deny custody or parenting time (more in the FAQ below).

## Lower-profile ways adults consume at home

If you’d rather keep cannabis out of the shared air at home, a few formats help, each with its own storage habit:

- **Low-dose edibles.** No smoke, but the biggest risk if a child finds them. Separate locked box, every time.
- **Vapes.** Usually less lingering smell than smoke, but cartridges are small and easy to misplace. Lock them up with the battery.
- **Tinctures.** Measured by the dropper. Close the child-resistant cap fully and store the bottle locked.

Our guides to [microdosing](/blog/microdosing-marijuana-thc-cbd/) and [discreet cannabis use](/blog/discreet-marijuana/) go deeper. For possession and home storage limits, see our [Michigan cannabis law guide](/cannabis-laws-by-state/michigan/), and our [FAQ](/faq/) covers common questions about cannabis in Michigan.

faq.q: Should I tell my kids I use cannabis?
faq.a: It’s your call, but avoid lying if they ask directly. Kids, especially teens, tend to find out, and honesty keeps your credibility for the conversations that matter most. Size the answer to their age, keep one message constant (cannabis is for adults only), and make sure your storage and habits match what you say.

faq.q: What should I do if my child eats an edible?
faq.a: Act right away. Take away anything left, keep the package, and call Poison Help at 1-800-222-1222 for guidance. If your child is hard to wake or struggling to breathe, call 911. Don’t wait for symptoms to appear, since edibles can take a while to act, and bring the packaging to any medical visit.

faq.q: Can I use cannabis while breastfeeding?
faq.a: The CDC advises against it, noting that chemicals from cannabis pass into breast milk. THC is also stored in body fat and released slowly, so a baby could still be exposed after a parent stops using. The agency encourages breastfeeding parents to avoid cannabis entirely. Talk with your doctor about your situation.

faq.q: How should I store cannabis at home?
faq.a: Use layers. Leave each product in the package it came in, and put those packages in a locked box or cabinet. Keep the box out of sight and reach, away from food and medicine. Lock up the extras, too: cartridges, leftover pre-rolls and empty packaging. In Michigan, more than 2.5 ounces at home must be kept locked.

faq.q: Can cannabis use affect custody in Michigan?
faq.a: Only in limited cases. Under Michigan’s adult-use law, a parent may not be denied custody or parenting time for legal cannabis use alone. The exception is use that creates an unreasonable danger to the child that can be clearly shown. Every case turns on its own facts, so if custody is in question, talk with a family law attorney.

review.summary: 22 claims checked: 17 ok, 5 fixed (0 wrong, 1 unsupported, 4 overstated).

review.notes: Independent fact-check, 2026-10-24. Tweet 2023 abstract re-read via NCBI E-utilities (every figure matches); CDC poisoning and pregnancy pages and the NIDA page reopened with WebFetch; Michigan statements matched to law-facts (mi-au-age, mi-au-home-storage, mi-au-custody, mi-au-vehicles-use, mi-edibles, mi-labeling, mi-med-physician); the two Michigan source URLs are the ones law-facts lists. Goodwin 2021 and Myran 2023 (E-utilities) verified two comparative lines and are recorded here only, keeping the list at six. Medical article: no shop, menu, deals or rewards link; links go to blog guides, /getting-a-medical-card/, /cannabis-laws-by-state/michigan/ and /faq/. Scripted lines for young children address the parent, not minors. Writer's notes: Medical brief: no shop, menu, deals or rewards link (the brief had none); no ordering section. No health claims for parents' use; no suggestion that use around children is safe; custody stated only as the law-facts claim, with a referral to a family law attorney. No storage product or brand named. "Weed" appears once, in an H2 carrying the secondary keyword. Poison Help number from the CDC page and the Michigan label rule. Cross-batch sweep 2026-10-24 (orchestrator, after the fact-check workflow): Michigan requires child-resistant packaging only for edible marihuana products (R 420.403(10); R 420.401(c) counts every infused product taken other than by inhalation, so drinks and tinctures too); R 420.501-508, including the R 420.504 label rule, set none for flower, vapes or concentrates (Cornell LII copies read 2026-10-24). Lines that said every product comes in child-resistant packaging now say original packaging.
